chapterTitle: When I Couldn't Stand It Any Longer — Timothy's Report and a Pastor's Prayer
themeTitle: “For Now We Live, If You Stand Fast in the Lord”

scripture.text: Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone,
scripture.understanding: “Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer” — μηκέτι στέγοντες. στέγω means to cover, to roof over, and so to hold in, to bear: like a roof that can no longer hold the weight of the rain. Paul's anxiety for the new church had reached breaking point. So he εὐδοκήσαμεν, “thought it good,” to be καταλειφθῆναι, “left behind,” at Athens μόνοι, “alone.” In the great intellectual capital of the ancient world, surrounded by idols (Acts 17:16), Paul chose loneliness so that the young church could be strengthened.

scripture.text: and sent Timothy, our brother and God’s servant in the Good News of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith;
scripture.understanding: He ἐπέμψαμεν, “sent,” Timothy, with two titles: ‘our brother’ and θεοῦ συνεργόν, literally ‘God's fellow worker’ (the WEB has “God’s servant”) in the gospel. A young man is given the highest dignity: working alongside God. His mission: στηρίξαι, “to establish” — to set firmly, to prop up, like a stake fixed in the ground — and παρακαλέσαι, “to comfort,” encourage, call alongside. New believers need both: a firm foundation and a warm encourager.

scripture.text: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you know that we are appointed to this task.
scripture.understanding: The purpose: “that no one be moved by these afflictions.” σαίνεσθαι is a vivid word: it describes a dog wagging its tail, and so being shaken, disturbed, or even coaxed and charmed away. Persecution can shake believers loose, or the easy road can lure them away. Then a startling statement: “we are appointed to this task” — εἰς τοῦτο κείμεθα, literally ‘we are laid down for this’. Affliction is not an accident; it is part of the calling of every believer (compare 2 Timothy 3:12).

scripture.text: For most certainly, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we are to suffer affliction, even as it happened, and you know.
scripture.understanding: Paul had προελέγομεν, “told you beforehand,” while he was with them, that μέλλομεν θλίβεσθαι, “we are to suffer affliction” — it was certain to come. And it did. Good discipleship does not promise new believers an easy life; it prepares them for trouble. Jesus did the same: “In the world you have oppression; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

scripture.text: For this cause I also, when I couldn’t stand it any longer, sent that I might know your faith, for fear that by any means the tempter had tempted you, and our labor would have been in vain.
scripture.understanding: Paul repeats verse 1 in the first person: “I also, when I couldn’t stand it any longer, sent that I might know your faith.” γνῶναι, ‘to know’ — γινώσκω, the word for coming to know by finding out, by experience. His fear: μή πως ἐπείρασεν ὑμᾶς ὁ πειράζων, “for fear that by any means the tempter had tempted you.” ὁ πειράζων is the same title used of Satan in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3). If the tempter had succeeded, “our labor” — κόπος, the exhausting toil of 2:9 — “would have been in vain” (κενόν, empty).

scripture.text: But when Timothy came just now to us from you, and brought us glad news of your faith and love, and that you have good memories of us always, longing to see us, even as we also long to see you;
scripture.understanding: “But when Timothy came just now” — ἄρτι, just this moment. Paul is writing almost as soon as Timothy arrived. And Timothy εὐαγγελισαμένου, “brought us glad news” — the very verb used for preaching the gospel. For Paul, news of their faith and love was itself a gospel. They had μνείαν ἀγαθήν, “good memories,” of Paul and were ἐπιποθοῦντες, “longing,” to see him, “even as we also long to see you.” The suspicion his enemies tried to sow had not taken root.

scripture.text: for this cause, brothers, we were comforted over you in all our distress and affliction through your faith.
scripture.understanding: The comforters are comforted. παρεκλήθημεν, “we were comforted,” in all our ἀνάγκῃ, “distress” — constraint, hardship, pressure from outside — and θλίψει, “affliction.” Paul was facing opposition in Corinth when Timothy arrived (Acts 18:5–6). And what comforted him was διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν πίστεως, “through your faith.” The strong apostle was strengthened by the weak young church.

scripture.text: For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.
scripture.understanding: “For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.” ζῶμεν, we live — Paul feels alive again. Their spiritual health was his life. στήκετε, “stand fast,” is a soldier holding his position under attack. The phrase ‘in the Lord’ tells you where the ground is: not in their own strength, but in Christ. A pastor's heart rises and falls with the faith of his people.

scripture.text: For what thanksgiving can we render again to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice for your sakes before our God;
scripture.understanding: Paul cannot find adequate thanks: τίνα γὰρ εὐχαριστίαν δυνάμεθα τῷ θεῷ ἀνταποδοῦναι, “For what thanksgiving can we render again to God for you?” The word means to give back in return, to repay. How do you repay God for this much joy? The joy itself is ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν, “before our God” — not just human relief, but joy experienced in God's presence.

scripture.text: night and day praying exceedingly that we may see your face, and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith?
scripture.understanding: A pray-family word: δεόμενοι, “praying” — the verb of δέησις, petition: earnest, specific asking out of need. And it is νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας, “night and day,” the same phrase used for Paul's work in 2:9. He worked night and day and prayed night and day. His two requests: to see their πρόσωπον, face, and καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν, “perfect that which is lacking in your faith.” καταρτίζω means to mend, to repair — the word used of fishermen mending their nets (Matthew 4:21). Their faith was real but incomplete; Paul wanted to mend the gaps.

scripture.text: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you;
scripture.understanding: The prayer of verses 11–13 begins. “Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you.” κατευθύναι, “direct” — make straight, clear the road — is singular in Greek, though it has two subjects: the Father and the Lord Jesus. Paul treats them as acting together as one, an early and natural witness to the deity of Christ. Satan blocked the road (2:18); Paul asks God to clear it.

scripture.text: and the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we also do toward you,
scripture.understanding: Two verbs for growth: πλεονάσαι, “increase” — have more and more — and περισσεύσαι, “abound” — overflow, exceed the measure. The object is ἀγάπη, the self-giving love of the love family, εἰς ἀλλήλους, “one toward another,” and εἰς πάντας, “toward all men” — not only fellow believers but even the neighbours persecuting them. And the model: “even as we also do toward you.” Paul prays that their love would overflow the way his overflows toward them.

scripture.text: to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
scripture.understanding: The goal of overflowing love: εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι, “to the end he may establish” (the same verb as Timothy's task in v. 2) your hearts ἀμέμπτους ἐν ἁγιωσύνῃ, “blameless in holiness.” Love is the path to holiness. And the time when this will be seen: ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ, “at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints” (ἁγίων) — the holy ones, which may mean angels, departed believers, or both. Chapter 3, like every chapter in this letter, ends at the return of Christ.

visualMeditations.title: The Roof That Could Not Hold
visualMeditations.image: Picture an old house in a long storm. Rain pounds the roof day after day. The beams creak, water begins to drip through, and finally the roof can hold no more. Now picture Paul in Athens, walking past temples and statues, unable to sleep. He thinks of the young believers he left behind in Thessalonica: mobs, threats, families turning against them, the tempter whispering. Weeks go by with no news. His heart is that roof, and finally it cannot hold the weight any longer. He sends away his only companion, Timothy, and stays alone in a city full of idols, just to know they are still standing.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone” (v. 1). The word στέγω pictures a roof that can no longer keep out the rain. Paul's love for the church weighed on him like a storm. Real spiritual leadership carries people's burdens in the heart. It does not stay detached. And it makes sacrifices — here, Paul's own companionship — for others' sake. Whose spiritual welfare weighs on you like that? If no one's, ask God to give you a heart that carries people.

visualMeditations.title: Mending the Nets
visualMeditations.image: Picture a fishing boat pulled up on the shore of the Sea of Galilee in the evening. Two brothers sit on the sand with a net spread across their knees. It has been used all night; there are tears where a rock caught it, loose knots where a big fish thrashed. They work through it carefully, hole by hole, so that tomorrow it will hold the catch. The net is not useless — it caught fish last night — but it is incomplete. Without mending, the next catch will slip away.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul prays “night and day praying exceedingly that we may see your face, and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith” (v. 10). The word καταρτίζω is used of mending nets. The Thessalonians' faith was real — Timothy's report proved it — but there were gaps: things they did not yet understand about holiness, about death, about the day of the Lord. Chapters 4 and 5 are Paul's mending work. Your faith may be genuine and still have holes. God is not ashamed of the gaps; He sends His word and His people to mend them.

visualMeditations.title: The Overflowing Cup
visualMeditations.image: Picture a clay cup set under a spring of water. At first the water just covers the bottom. Then it rises. Soon it reaches the brim, and then it overflows, running down the sides onto the ground around it and soaking into the dry earth. The cup does not try to overflow; it simply stays under the spring. Now picture a small church in a hostile city, whose love for one another keeps growing until it spills out onto the neighbours who mock them, the officials who threaten them, and strangers passing through.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul prays, “the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we also do toward you” (v. 12). The two verbs mean to have more and more, and then to overflow. Christian love is meant to spill beyond the church to everyone, even enemies. And it comes from the Lord, the spring. The result is holiness: “to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints” (v. 13). Stay under the spring, and the overflow will come.

structure.label: Timothy Sent From Athens (v. 1-5)
structure.body: Unable to bear the uncertainty, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen and encourage the Thessalonians, so that afflictions would not shake them — afflictions Paul had warned them were certain — and to learn whether the tempter had undone their faith.

structure.label: Timothy's Good News (v. 6-8)
structure.body: Timothy returned with glad news of their faith, love and affection for Paul; in all his own distress Paul was comforted, and he feels alive again because they are standing firm in the Lord.

structure.label: Thanksgiving and Longing (v. 9-10)
structure.body: Paul cannot thank God enough for the joy they give him, and he prays earnestly night and day to see them and to supply what is lacking in their faith.

structure.label: A Prayer for Love and Holiness (v. 11-13)
structure.body: Paul prays that God the Father and the Lord Jesus would clear his way to them, make their love increase and overflow, and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all His saints.

sections.heading: Love That Could Not Wait
paragraphs: Acts tells part of the story behind chapter 3. After Thessalonica, Paul was driven out of Berea as well, and the believers took him by sea to Athens (Acts 17:14–15). He sent word for Silas and Timothy to join him quickly. Paul then sent Timothy back to Thessalonica, while he himself stayed in Athens — the city where he preached on the Areopagus — and later moved on to Corinth. Chapter 3 lets us see what was going on inside Paul during those weeks. “Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone” (v. 1).

Timothy's assignment was “to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith; that no one be moved by these afflictions” (vv. 2–3). Paul was not surprised by the persecution; he had predicted it: “For most certainly, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we are to suffer affliction, even as it happened, and you know” (v. 4). He taught the same in Galatia: “through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom” (Acts 14:22). Persecution is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is one of the normal conditions of following a rejected Messiah: “all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12).

But Paul knew the real danger was not the pain; it was the tempter. “I also, when I couldn’t stand it any longer, sent that I might know your faith, for fear that by any means the tempter had tempted you, and our labor would have been in vain” (v. 5). Satan uses suffering to whisper that God has abandoned you, that faith is not worth the cost, that you should go back to the old life. Paul's response was practical love: he sent help. Jesus did the same for Peter: “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

sections.heading: Good News About Good News
paragraphs: Then Timothy came back — and the letter seems to have been written almost immediately: “But when Timothy came just now to us from you, and brought us glad news of your faith and love” (v. 6). The verb for ‘brought glad news’ is εὐαγγελίζω, the word normally used for preaching the gospel. Timothy's report of their faith was gospel to Paul's ears. The church was standing. They remembered him with love and longed to see him. The rumours against him had failed.

The effect on Paul was dramatic. “For this cause, brothers, we were comforted over you in all our distress and affliction through your faith” (v. 7). Paul was in Corinth, facing fresh opposition (Acts 18:5–6). The young church's faith strengthened the veteran apostle. Then comes one of the most moving lines Paul ever wrote: “For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord” (v. 8). Paul's life was bound up with theirs. He did not measure his ministry by crowds or comfort but by whether believers stood firm.

Thanksgiving overflows: “For what thanksgiving can we render again to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice for your sakes before our God” (v. 9). And it immediately becomes prayer: “night and day praying exceedingly that we may see your face, and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith” (v. 10). Joy over their progress does not make Paul complacent. Their faith is genuine but incomplete, like a net that needs mending. Thanksgiving and concern belong together in a pastor's prayers.

sections.heading: Increase, Abound, Be Established
paragraphs: The chapter ends with a prayer that forms the bridge to the second half of the letter. First, Paul asks: “Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you” (v. 11). Satan had hindered him (2:18); now he asks God to clear the road. In Greek the verb ‘direct’ is singular, though it has two subjects. Without explaining it, Paul speaks of the Father and the Lord Jesus as one actor — a quiet but powerful witness, in one of the earliest Christian documents, to the full deity of Christ.

Second: “and the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we also do toward you” (v. 12). Love is the theme of chapter 4:9–12, and Paul prays for it before he teaches it. He wants their love to grow and then overflow its banks — to fellow believers and to ‘all men’, including those persecuting them. Jesus said, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Love that stops at the church door is too small.

Third, and the purpose of it all: “to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints” (v. 13). Holiness is the theme of 4:1–8, and the coming of the Lord is the theme of 4:13–5:11. In one sentence Paul has previewed the rest of the letter. The link is important: love leads to holiness, and holiness prepares us for His coming. The God who began the work is the One who establishes the heart, as Paul wrote elsewhere: “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

ntConnection.heading: Strengthening the Brothers
paragraphs: Timothy's mission ‘to establish’ uses the same verb Jesus used for Peter. Before Peter's denial, Jesus warned him: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat” (Luke 22:31), and then promised, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Satan the tempter attacks faith; Jesus intercedes; and restored believers strengthen others. That is the pattern of 1 Thessalonians 3: the tempter threatened, Paul prayed, Timothy went to establish them.

The warning that suffering is normal runs through the New Testament. Paul told new disciples “that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom” (Acts 14:22). Peter wrote, “Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you, to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you” (1 Peter 4:12). And Jesus Himself said, “In the world you have oppression; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Paul was faithful to this teaching from the first weeks of a church's life.

Paul's prayer for overflowing love echoes his prayer for the Philippians: “This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment” (Philippians 1:9). And the word ‘perfect’ in verse 10 — mending what is lacking — is the same word used for the work of church leaders: “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). Paul wants each believer complete; as he told the Colossians, “that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Colossians 1:28).

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to roof over, i.e. (figuratively) to cover with silence (endure patiently).” The picture is a roof that keeps out the rain. In 1 Corinthians 13:7 love “bears all things” with this word — covering and protecting. Here Paul uses it negatively: he could no longer hold the pressure in. His love for the Thessalonians was so strong that not knowing how they were became unbearable. Pastoral love is not cool detachment. It feels the weight of people's struggles.

Strong's: “to set fast, i.e. (literally) to turn resolutely in a certain direction, or (figuratively) to confirm.” It pictures fixing something firmly in place, like a stake driven into the ground or a building on a foundation. Timothy was sent to do it (v. 2), and Paul prays that God will do it (v. 13). Jesus told Peter to ‘establish your brothers’ (Luke 22:32). New believers are not meant to be left to themselves; God strengthens them through His people and by His own hand.

Strong's: “to wag (as a dog its tail fawningly), i.e. (generally) to shake (figuratively, disturb).” It is used only here in the New Testament. The picture can be of being shaken by trouble, or of being charmed and coaxed away, like a dog wagging toward whoever offers food. Persecution can shake you; the promise of an easier life can lure you. Paul sent Timothy to make sure neither happened. Ask yourself which danger you are more exposed to: being shaken, or being coaxed away.

Strong's: “to complete thoroughly, i.e. repair (literally or figuratively) or adjust.” It is used of James and John “mending their nets” (Matthew 4:21), of restoring a believer caught in a fault (Galatians 6:1), and of God making believers “complete in every good work” (Hebrews 13:21). It does not mean that the Thessalonians' faith was false; it means that it had gaps to be repaired. Growth in Christ is often less about adding something new and more about mending what is torn.

Strong's: “sacredness (i.e. properly, the quality).” It is related to ἅγιος, holy, and ἁγιασμός, sanctification (4:3). ἁγιωσύνη describes the state of being holy, set apart for God and morally pure. Paul prays that the Thessalonians' hearts will be established ‘blameless in holiness’ at Jesus' coming. Holiness is not mainly about rules; it is the condition of a heart that belongs wholly to God. And it grows, as verse 12 shows, out of overflowing love.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: how you carry the people God has given you, how you face affliction, and what is still lacking in your faith.

items.title: Whom Are You Carrying?
items.body: Paul's love for the Thessalonians became an unbearable weight until he knew they were safe. The Spirit may be asking whether there is anyone you carry like that — someone newer in faith, a struggling friend, a child, a small group. Or He may be stirring that weight in you now for a particular person. Do not ignore it. Like Paul, act on it: pray, send a message, visit, send someone who can help. Spiritual love is meant to move you to action.

items.title: You Were Told Beforehand
items.body: Paul had warned the Thessalonians that affliction would come. Perhaps no one warned you, and when hardship hit, you felt betrayed by God. The Spirit wants to reframe your trouble: “we are appointed to this task” (v. 3). Suffering for Christ is not a sign that you are outside His will. Ask Him to show you where the tempter has used your affliction to make you doubt God's love, and to establish your heart again in the truth.

items.title: What Is Lacking?
items.body: Paul prayed to “perfect that which is lacking in your faith” (v. 10). Your faith may be real and still have gaps: an area of life you have not surrendered, a truth you have not understood, a fear you have not faced, a habit you have not broken. The Spirit is a gentle net-mender. Ask Him to show you one gap in your faith, and to begin repairing it through His word and His people.

audit.title: The Burden Check
audit.body: Write down the names of the people whose spiritual welfare you genuinely care about. Next to each, write when you last prayed for them by name and when you last made contact. Choose one to reach out to this week, as Paul sent Timothy (v. 2).

audit.title: The Affliction Check
audit.body: Think of a current pressure or hardship you are facing because you follow Christ. Has it moved you closer to God, or has the tempter used it to pull you away (vv. 3–5)? Write one honest sentence about it and bring it to God in prayer.

audit.title: The Overflow Check
audit.body: Paul prays for love that overflows ‘toward all men’ (v. 12). List the people outside your church or circle of friends whom you find hardest to love. Choose one and decide on a concrete act of love toward them this week.

practices.title: Be Someone's Timothy
practices.body: Timothy was sent to strengthen and encourage believers under pressure. This week, identify one believer who is going through a hard time — illness, persecution, grief, doubt or loneliness. Contact them in person if possible. Listen first. Then share one Scripture that has strengthened you, and pray with them. Afterwards, send them a short follow-up message. Ask God to make you someone who establishes others, so that no one is moved by these afflictions.

practices.title: Pray Paul's Prayer
practices.body: Use verses 11–13 as a prayer every day for a week, for yourself and for three other people. Ask the Father and the Lord Jesus to direct your path, to make your love increase and overflow toward one another and toward all people, and to establish your hearts blameless in holiness before God at the coming of the Lord Jesus. At the end of the week, write down how praying for overflowing love and holiness has changed the way you see those people.

prayerReflection: “Father, give me a heart like Paul's, that carries Your people with real love and cannot rest until I know they are standing firm. Make me willing to be left alone if it means others are strengthened. Thank You for those who were sent to establish and comfort me. When affliction comes, keep me from being shaken or coaxed away. Remind me that I was told beforehand and that I am appointed to this path. Guard me against the tempter, who wants to use suffering to make me doubt Your love. Let me live because others stand firm in You, and let me stand firm so that others may live. I cannot thank You enough for the joy of seeing faith grow. Mend what is lacking in my faith. Our God and Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct my way. Make my love increase and overflow toward my brothers and sisters and toward all people. Establish my heart blameless in holiness before You at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: Paul Alone in Athens
storyConnections.summary: After being driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, Paul was taken to Athens and waited there for Silas and Timothy. Walking through the city, he was deeply troubled to see it full of idols. He reasoned in the synagogue and in the marketplace every day, and the philosophers brought him to the Areopagus, where he preached about the unknown God, the Creator who does not live in temples made with hands, who commands all people everywhere to repent and who has given proof of coming judgment by raising Jesus from the dead. Some mocked, some wanted to hear more, and a few believed. This is the setting of 1 Thessalonians 3:1 — ‘left behind at Athens alone’. While Paul preached to philosophers, his heart was with a small persecuted church in Macedonia.

storyConnections.title: Jesus Prays for Peter
storyConnections.summary: At the Last Supper, Jesus warned Peter: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat” (Luke 22:31). Then He gave him a promise and a commission: “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Peter insisted that he would go to prison and death with Jesus, but Jesus told him he would deny Him three times before the rooster crowed. Peter fell, but his faith did not finally fail, and he went on to strengthen the church. Paul's fear in 1 Thessalonians 3:5 — that the tempter might have tempted them — and his sending of Timothy ‘to establish’ them follow the same pattern: Satan attacks faith, Christ intercedes, and restored believers strengthen others.

storyConnections.title: Timothy, a Young Fellow Worker
storyConnections.summary: Timothy was a young disciple from Lystra, with a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers in Lystra and Iconium. Paul wanted him to join the mission team, and he travelled with Paul and Silas through the churches, delivering the decisions of the Jerusalem council. The result: the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew in number daily. Within months this young man was trusted with a dangerous solo mission to a persecuted church in Thessalonica. Paul calls him ‘our brother and God's fellow worker’ (3:2). Timothy's faithfulness on that mission, and his good report, gave Paul new life. Years later Paul would write two letters to him, still calling him his true child in the faith.
